title: The Byzantine Empire was founded.
desc: The Byzantine Empire (c. 330–1453) was the long-lasting eastern continuation of the Roman Empire, centered in Constantinople. It served as a major power in the Mediterranean, preserving Greek and Roman knowledge while embracing Eastern Orthodox Christianity.

title: Russia declared its first draft
desc: Russia declared that it was initiating a 'partial mobilization' of military reservists to bolster the country's war effort against Ukraine.

title: A Turkish Airlines plane carrying 113 people from Albania to Turkey was hijacked
desc: Turkish Airlines Flight 1476, a Turkish Airlines plane carrying 113 people from Tirana, Albania to Istanbul, Turkey, was hijacked, but lands at Italy's Brindisi Airport. The hijackers surrendered and were arrested by Italian police.

title: US scientists win Nobel Prize in Physics for research in cosmic background radiation.
desc: United States scientists John C. Mather and George Smoot win the Nobel Prize in Physics for research into cosmic microwave background radiation that helps explain the origins of galaxies and stars.

title: Russia invaded Ukraine
desc: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, marking the largest conflict in Europe since World War II. Following President Vladimir Putin's announcement of a 'special military operation,' Russian forces entered from Russia, Belarus, and Crimea, targeting cities nationwide and aiming to capture Kyiv.

title: A&W Root Beer was founded
desc: A&W Root Beer was created by Roy W. Allen, who introduced his signature beverage at a roadside stand in Lodi, California, on June 20 of that year. Allen later partnered with Frank Wright in 1922 to trademark the brand name 'A&W'.

title: World War I ended
desc: World War I officially ended with the signing of the armistice between the Allies and Germany on November 11, 1918, at 11:00 a.m. (the 'eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month'), ending the fighting on the Western Front. While this date is recognized as the end of the war, formal peace treaties were signed later, such as the Treaty of Versailles on June 28, 1919.

title: World War I begins
desc: On July 28, 1914, one month after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. This pivotal action, initiated by a telegram from Vienna to Belgrade, triggered the alliance system and escalated the conflict into World War I. Germany had previously given 'blank cheque' support, while Russia pledged to defend Serbia.

title: The St. Bartholomew Massacre happened
desc: The Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572 was a targeted group of assassinations and a wave of Catholic mob violence directed against the Huguenots during the French Wars of Religion.

title: Six men raised the US flag on Iwo Jima
desc: On February 23, 1945, during the Battle of Iwo Jima, U.S. Marines raised two flags atop Mount Suribachi. The second, larger flag-raising was captured in Joe Rosenthal’s iconic Pulitzer Prize-winning photograph, symbolizing victory and sacrifice. The event, featuring six men, boosted morale during the 36-day battle.

title: Bob Marley was born
desc: Bob Marley was born on February 6, 1945, in Nine Mile, Saint Ann Parish, Jamaica, to Cedella Malcolm and Norval Sinclair Marley. He grew up in rural Jamaica and later moved to Trench Town at age 9. His birthplace is now a popular tourist attraction known as the 'Spirit of Reggae'.

title: MacArthur announces Manila's capture, 5,000 prisoners liberated
desc: General Douglas MacArthur announced the capture of Manila and the liberation of 5,000 prisoners. Yugoslav Partisans began the Mostar operation.

title: This site was created
desc: I had the idea to make this in 2022, but I didn't know how to use HTML, CSS, and JS to make it–only Python. On March 12th 2026, I was looking through my ideas list and realized I can make this, so I did.

title: William Herschel sees what he thinks is a comet but actually discovers the planet Uranus
desc: On March 13, 1781, astronomer William Herschel discovered Uranus while surveying stars in Gemini with a home-built telescope. Initially believing the object was a comet due to its movement, further observations of its near-circular orbit confirmed it was a new planet. Herschel proposed naming it Georgium Sidus (George’s Star) after King George III, though it was later named Uranus by Johann Bode.

title: Karl Friedrich Schinkel was born
desc: Prussian architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel (1781–1841) was a leading figure in Neoclassical and Gothic Revival architecture, best known for his iconic buildings in Berlin. His Altes Museum became a model for national art museums worldwide, and his Bauakademie is considered a forerunner of modern architecture.

title: The Massacre of Vassy happened
desc: The Massacre of Vassy Frenc: massacre de Wassy) was the murder of Huguenot worshippers and citizens in an armed action by troops of the Duke of Guise, in Wassy, France on 1 March 1562. The massacre is identified as the first major event in the French Wars of Religion.

title: Germany invaded Poland, marking the beginning of WWII
desc: World War II officially began on September 1, 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, prompting Britain and France to declare war on Germany two days later, on September 3, 1939. While this is the widely accepted date, some historians consider earlier conflicts, such as the 1937 Japanese invasion of China, as the start.

title: Parisian revolutionaries stormed the Bastille, kicking off the French Revolution
desc: On July 14, 1789, Parisian revolutionaries stormed the Bastille, a medieval fortress and prison symbolizing royal tyranny, to seize gunpowder and weapons. Defecting French Guards and angry citizens overwhelmed the garrison, marking a decisive victory against King Louis XVI and accelerating the French Revolution, which is still celebrated annually on this date.

title: Four commercial planes hijacked and crashed into New York's World Trade Center towers in the deadliest terrorist attack in American history
desc: The September 11 attacks, colloquially known as 9/11, were a series of coordinated Islamic terrorist suicide attacks perpetrated by al-Qaeda against the United States in 2001. Nineteen terrorists hijacked four airliners, then flew one into each of the Twin Towers at the World Trade Center in New York City.

title: Salvador Allende was overthrown by CIA-backed coup in Chile
desc: On September 11, 1973, Chilean armed forces led by General Augusto Pinochet overthrew President Salvador Allende’s democratically elected Marxist government in a violent coup.

title: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Pompeii
desc: In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius, a stratovolcano located in the modern-day region of Campania, erupted, causing one of the deadliest eruptions in history.

title: Sharon Stouder won four Olympic medals as a 15-year-old swimmer in 1964
desc: American swimmer Sharon Stouder sets a world record of 1:04.7 to beat Ada Kok of the Netherlands by 0.9 seconds and win the women's 100 m butterfly at the Tokyo Olympics

title: The War of 1812 started
desc: The War of 1812 officially began on June 18, 1812, when U.S. President James Madison signed a declaration of war against Great Britain. The conflict was declared following tensions over maritime rights, trade blockades, and British support for Native American tribes against U.S. expansion

title: The American Revolutionary War happened
desc: In 1776, the American colonies declared independence from Great Britain, officially adopting the Declaration of Independence on July 4th and transforming the rebellion into the Revolutionary War. Key events included the British evacuation of Boston, the challenging New York campaign, the publication of Thomas Paine’s Common Sense, and Washington’s surprise crossing of the Delaware River.

title: US drops atomic bomb on Hiroshima, killing 80,000 instantly
desc: The US B-29 bomber Enola Gay dropped an atomic bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" on Hiroshima, Japan at 8:15 AM. The blast, equivalent to 15,000 tons of TNT, reduced four square miles of the city to ruins and immediately killed 80,000 people.

title: Berlin Wall falls as East Germany opens its borders
desc: The fall of the Berlin Wall. East Germany announced that citizens could cross the border freely, and crowds began tearing the wall down that night, effectively ending the division of Germany after 28 years.

title: 100-year flood submerges Prague's historic Kampa district
desc: A 100-year flood of the Vltava River peaked at Prague, submerging the historic Kampa district under several yards of water, flooding the Prague Zoo, and killing multiple animals including an elephant, five rhinoceroses, and a lion.

title: Former Queen Juliana of the Netherlands dies aged 94
desc: Queen Juliana of the Netherlands (1909–2004) reigned from 1948 to 1980, when she abdicated in favor of her daughter Beatrix. Known for her down-to-earth, approachable style, she was widely beloved by the Dutch people and was active in social welfare causes throughout her reign. She died on March 20, 2004, her 94th birthday.

title: Monkeypox declared global health emergency by WHO
desc: The monkeypox outbreak is declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by the World Health Organization.

title: Israel officially hands over Jericho to Palestinian control.
desc: Israel formally hands Jericho to Palestinian Authority control, which is likely to strengthen Mahmoud Abbas. The PA will resume security control over the city and will have to make sure that wanted militants will remain in check.

title: Subnautica 2 was released for early access
desc: Subnautica 2 is an open-world underwater survival game where you play as an Alterra colonist stranded on a mysterious, uncharted oceanic world. After your colony ship crashes, you must scavenge for resources, craft tools, build bases, and unravel deep sci-fi mysteries while surviving deadly alien wildlife.

title: The European Space Agency's Huygens probe successfully landed on Titan, Saturn's largest moon.
desc: In what is expected to be one of the major scientific events of this decade, the Huygens probe successfully lands on Saturn's largest moon Titan. Data sent back from the probe via the Cassini orbiter is now being analysed. Three low-resolution pictures have been released, including one from an altitude of 16 km that appears to show channels cut by liquid, and another from the surface of Titan showing rocks or ice.

title: Al Stevens was born
desc: A C programmer, jazz musician, and ventriloquist from Maryland. He wrote the C Programming column for Dr. Dobb's Journal for 15 years and authored over two dozen programming books before retiring to Florida, where he wrote mystery novels and played jazz. His personal website, built in his 60s, still quietly exists.

title: Dr. Dobb's Journal was founded
desc: The first regular periodical focused on microcomputer software rather than hardware. Originally titled "Dr. Dobb's Journal of Tiny BASIC Calisthenics & Orthodontia — Running Light without Overbyte," it became one of the most influential magazines in programming history. Al Stevens (see 06/24/1940) wrote its C Programming column for 15 years.

title: The robots.txt standard was proposed
desc: Martijn Koster proposed the Robots Exclusion Protocol while working for Nexor, establishing the standard that tells web crawlers which pages to avoid. Though technically just a suggestion with no enforcement mechanism, it became universally adopted and remains unchanged today — accidentally serving as a roadmap of sensitive paths for anyone curious enough to look.

title: Stockton University became recognized as a university
desc: Stockton officially became a university on February 18, 2015, when its Board of Trustees voted to change the institution's official designation and name from The Richard Stockton College of New Jersey to Stockton University. The public institution, located in Galloway Township, New Jersey, was originally founded as South Jersey State College in 1969 and opened its doors to students in 1971.

title: The IRS was formed
desc: The IRS was created in three main stages: first established as the Office of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue in 1862, expanded after the 16th Amendment in 1913, and officially renamed the Internal Revenue Service in 1953.

title: The first man, Neil Armstrong (USA), stepped on the moon
desc: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface at 10:56 PM EDT (02:56 UTC on July 21), speaking the famous words: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

title: Smallpox was eradicated
desc: On May 8, 1980, the World Health Organization formally declared smallpox eradicated, making it the first and only human disease ever completely eliminated through deliberate global effort. The coordinated vaccination campaign, spanning over a decade and dozens of countries, is widely regarded as one of the greatest public health achievements in history.

title: France's gift to America dedicated in New York Harbor
desc: The Statue of Liberty, a gift from the people of France, was dedicated in New York Harbor on October 28, 1886. Designed by French sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi, the statue was dismantled into 350 individual pieces, packed in 214 crates, and shipped to New York where it was reassembled on a pedestal designed by architect Richard Morris Hunt. Of the more than 2,000 attendees at the formal dedication, only two women were invited — members of the Women's Suffrage Association chartered their own boat in protest and hung banners in defense of women's rights.

title: Wright Brothers achieve first powered flight at Kitty Hawk
desc: Orville and Wilbur Wright, two self-taught engineers, achieved controlled powered flight for the first time on December 17, 1903. Although their aircraft flew for just 12 seconds and covered only 120 feet, it was a groundbreaking achievement that revolutionized transportation and forever changed how humans see the world.

title: Five Guys Foods UK Limited was incorporated
desc: Five Guys Foods UK Limited is an active company incorporated on 12 March 2013 with the registered office located in London, Greater London. Five Guys Foods UK Limited was registered 13 years ago.

title: The first iPhone was released
desc: The first iPhone release marked a revolutionary moment in technology, blending a touchscreen mobile phone, an iPod, and an internet communicator into a single device. It fundamentally transformed the smartphone industry and redefined how the world interacts with mobile software and hardware.

title: The Declaration of Independence was signed
desc: Members of the Continental Congress officially began signing the engrossed parchment copy of the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia. While the document was adopted on July 4, this was the pivotal moment when delegates risked their lives and property by putting their signatures to the rebellion against Great Britain.

title: Nelson Mandela was elected President of South Africa
desc: In South Africa (Johannesburg): Newly elected President Nelson Mandela gave his triumphant first State of the Nation address to the first democratically elected, post-apartheid parliament. It marked the definitive, official dawn of the "Rainbow Nation" on the global political stage.

title: O.J. Simpson fled the police while being streamed live to 95 million viewers
desc: As the 1994 FIFA World Cup officially kicked off in Chicago with the opening match between Germany and Bolivia, a surreal crisis unfolded in Los Angeles. Former football star O.J. Simpson fled murder charges in a white Ford Bronco, sparking a slow-speed police chase watched live by 95 million concurrent viewers.

title: Mubarak calls for Egypt's first multi-candidate presidential elections
desc: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak called for parliament to amend the constitution to allow for direct, secret elections for the next president on February 26, 2005 — a significant moment that was seen as a rare democratic opening in Egypt, though critics noted the elections still had severe restrictions. It came years before the Arab Spring would ultimately force him from power in 2011.

title: Sarbanes-Oxley Act establishes PCAOB to oversee public company audits
desc: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) was established on July 30, 2002, through the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, passed in the wake of major accounting scandals at Enron and WorldCom. The PCAOB was created to oversee audits of publicly traded US companies, setting auditing standards and conducting inspections of registered accounting firms — functions previously self-regulated by the accounting profession itself through the AICPA.

title: USS Vincennes shoots down Iran Air Flight 655, killing all 290 aboard
desc: During the Iran–Iraq War, the US Navy cruiser USS Vincennes fired two missiles at Iran Air Flight 655, an Airbus A300 on a routine civilian route from Bandar Abbas to Dubai. The crew had misidentified it as an attacking F-14 fighter. All 290 people on board died, including 65 children. The US later admitted the ship was inside Iranian waters, expressed regret without formally apologizing, and in 1996 paid $61.8 million to the victims' families as part of an ICJ settlement.

title: Hubble Space Telescope launched
desc: Space Shuttle Discovery carried the telescope into orbit on mission STS-31, starting more than three decades of observations from above the atmosphere.

title: James Webb Space Telescope launches from French Guiana
desc: An Ariane 5 rocket carried the James Webb Space Telescope into space from Kourou, French Guiana. The telescope has a 6.5-meter segmented mirror and observes in infrared, which lets it see some of the earliest galaxies. It traveled to a point about 1.5 million km from Earth and released its first full-color images in July 2022.

title: Fire destroys the roof and spire of Notre-Dame de Paris
desc: A fire broke out in the attic of Notre-Dame cathedral on the evening of April 15, 2019, and burned through most of the medieval wooden roof. The spire collapsed about an hour after the fire was first reported. Firefighters saved the main stone structure, including the twin bell towers, and the fire was out by the next morning. The cathedral reopened to the public in December 2024 after a five-year restoration.

title: Musical.ly shuts down and merges into TikTok
desc: ByteDance folded Musical.ly, the lip-sync app popular with teenagers, into its own TikTok app on August 2, 2018. Musical.ly’s roughly 100 million monthly users were moved over automatically with an app update, keeping their accounts and videos. TikTok already had around 500 million users at that point. ByteDance had bought Musical.ly in November 2017 for a reported $800 million to $1 billion, and the merger ended the Musical.ly brand and made TikTok a single app for everywhere outside China.

title: Instagram launches on the iOS App Store
desc: Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger released Instagram as an iPhone photo-sharing app with filters and a square crop. It had one million registered users within two months. Facebook announced it was buying the company for $1 billion in cash and stock in April 2012, when it had about 30 million users.

title: Spain beats Argentina in extra time to win the 2026 World Cup
desc: Spain won the 2026 FIFA World Cup final 1-0 over defending champions Argentina at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The match was scoreless after 90 minutes, and substitute Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute. It was Spain’s second World Cup title, after 2010, and it ended Argentina’s attempt to become the first team since Brazil in 1962 to retain the trophy. This was the first World Cup with 48 teams, hosted jointly by the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

title: William Shatner is born in Montreal
desc: William Shatner was born in Montreal, Quebec, on March 22, 1931. The Canadian actor became famous as Captain James T. Kirk in the original Star Trek series (1966 to 1969) and later starred in T.J. Hooker and Boston Legal. In the late 1990s he became the pitchman for Priceline.com and took company stock instead of cash for the ads, though Priceline’s CEO has denied the widely repeated claim that the stock made him $600 million. In October 2021, at age 90, he flew on Blue Origin’s New Shepard rocket and became the oldest person to travel to space up to that point.

title: Hurricane Ivan devastates Grenada
desc: Hurricane Ivan passed just south of Grenada on September 7, 2004, as a strong Category 3 storm with winds of about 125 mph. About 90% of the island's houses were damaged, 39 people died, and roughly 18,000 were left homeless. Nearly every major building in the capital, St. George's, was damaged or destroyed, including the parliament building. The damage came to about $1.1 billion, roughly twice Grenada's annual GDP, and the island lost about 80% of its nutmeg crop, its main agricultural export. Ivan later reached Category 5 and went on to hit Jamaica, the Cayman Islands, and the US Gulf Coast.

title: Jef Raskin, who started Apple's Macintosh project, dies at 61
desc: Jef Raskin, the human-computer interface expert who conceived the Macintosh project at Apple in 1979, died of pancreatic cancer in Pacifica, California, on February 26, 2005. He had been diagnosed in December 2004. Steve Jobs took over the project after about a year, and the finished Mac looked very different from Raskin's text-only, keyboard-driven vision. Raskin left Apple in 1982 and went on to design the Canon Cat, write The Humane Interface (2000), and begin work on the Archy interface.

title: US military deaths in Iraq pass 1,000, by AP count
desc: On September 7, 2004, the number of US service members killed in Iraq passed 1,000 in an Associated Press tally, about 18 months after the March 2003 invasion. The milestone came after two days of heavy fighting, including clashes with Shiite militia loyal to Muqtada al-Sadr in Baghdad's Sadr City, that killed 14 American troops. The Pentagon's own count that day was 997, and the White House said it mourned every death regardless of the number. Nearly 7,000 US troops had been wounded by then.

title: Wales beat France in Paris on the way to a first Grand Slam since 1978
desc: Wales beat France 24-18 at the Stade de France in the third round of the Six Nations, keeping their perfect record after earlier wins over England and Italy. Few had expected much from the Welsh side coming into the tournament. They went on to clinch the Grand Slam on March 19 by beating Ireland 32-20 in Cardiff, Wales' first Grand Slam since 1978 and their first Triple Crown since 1988.

title: Spotify launches in Europe
desc: Spotify launched its music streaming service in several European markets on October 7, 2008. The Swedish company, founded in 2006 by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon, was conceived as a legal alternative to music piracy. It reached the United States in July 2011 and went public on the New York Stock Exchange in April 2018.

title: Stockton University receives largest gift in its history, $8 million from the Scarpa Foundation
desc: Stockton University, a public university in southern New Jersey with campuses in Galloway and Atlantic City, announced an $8 million pledge from the John F. Scarpa Foundation, the largest gift in its history. The money will expand Atlantic City academic programs and the Galloway health sciences program, with the rest going to an unrestricted fund. Trustees unanimously voted the day before to name two buildings for donor John F. Scarpa: the Academic Center in Atlantic City and the Health Sciences Center in Galloway.

title: Norway's Karsten Warholm breaks his own 400m hurdles world record to win Olympic gold in Tokyo
desc: Norway's Karsten Warholm won the men's 400m hurdles at the Tokyo Olympics in 45.94 seconds, breaking his own world record by 0.76 seconds and becoming the first person to run under 46 seconds. American Rai Benjamin took silver in 46.17, which also beat Warholm's previous record of 46.70 set a month earlier in Oslo, and Brazil's Alison dos Santos took bronze in 46.72. Six of the eight finalists set a world, continental, or national record.

title: Valve releases Dota 2 out of beta as a free-to-play game
desc: Valve took Dota 2 out of beta on July 9, 2013, opening the free-to-play game to every Steam user after about two years of closed and open testing. It was the standalone sequel to the Defense of the Ancients mod, led by the mod's longtime designer IceFrog. Demand was high enough that Valve set up a launch queue to bring new players in waves.

title: Intuit goes public on Nasdaq a year after launching QuickBooks
desc: Intuit, the software company founded in 1983 by Scott Cook and Tom Proulx, went public on the Nasdaq under the ticker INTU. It had launched QuickBooks, its small-business accounting software, the year before. Later that year it acquired ChipSoft, the maker of TurboTax.

title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies at 34
desc: RJ Mitte, who played Walter White Jr. on Breaking Bad across all five seasons, died at 34 in Brownsville, Texas. Diagnosed with cerebral palsy as a child, he became a prominent disability rights advocate and also worked as a model and film producer. His representatives confirmed he died by suicide.

title: Breaking Bad premieres on AMC
desc: AMC premiered Breaking Bad, written and directed by creator Vince Gilligan, with Bryan Cranston as Walter White, a chemistry teacher turned meth manufacturer. The pilot drew about 1.41 million viewers, a modest start for a show whose 2013 finale drew 10.28 million.

title: Dragon Ball Z premieres on Fuji TV
desc: Dragon Ball Z, the sequel to Dragon Ball, adapted Akira Toriyama's manga and premiered on Fuji TV, taking over its predecessor's time slot. It ran for 291 episodes until 1996. US audiences didn't see it until an edited dub began airing in syndication in September 1996.

title: BlizzCon, Blizzard's fan convention, holds its first show in Anaheim
desc: Blizzard Entertainment held the first BlizzCon, a two-day fan convention for its Warcraft, StarCraft, and Diablo games, at the Anaheim Convention Center in California. Tickets cost $120, and the show featured World of Warcraft's first expansion, The Burning Crusade. There was no BlizzCon in 2006, and the event returned in 2007.

title: Stockton union establishes SFT Solidarity Park
desc: SFT Solidarity Park was established at Stockton University, a public university in southern New Jersey, to honor those committed to a fair and equitable workplace "from the Podium to the Pine." A plaque credits the Stockton Federation of Teachers, Librarians and Professional Staff, Local 2275 of the AFT.

title: Mac DeMarco releases This Old Dog
desc: Mac DeMarco, a Canadian singer-songwriter known for laid-back indie rock, released This Old Dog, his first album in three years, on Captured Tracks. Finished around his move from New York to Los Angeles, it leans on acoustic guitar, synthesizers, and a drum machine for a more mature sound.

title: Sleep Token releases Even in Arcadia
desc: Sleep Token, an anonymous British band that blends metal, R&B, and electronic music and performs in masks and cloaks, released Even in Arcadia, its fourth album and first for RCA Records. It debuted at number one on the US Billboard 200 with 127,000 first-week units, the biggest streaming week ever for a hard rock album.

title: Nickelback releases Silver Side Up
desc: Nickelback, a Canadian post-grunge rock band, released Silver Side Up, its third album, the same day as the 9/11 attacks. Its single "How You Remind Me" reached number one on the US Billboard Hot 100, and the album was certified double platinum in the US by the end of 2001.

title: Hurricane Irene makes landfall in North Carolina
desc: Hurricane Irene, the first hurricane of the 2011 Atlantic season, came ashore near Cape Lookout on North Carolina’s Outer Banks as a Category 1 storm, killing five people in the state. It made a second landfall in New Jersey the next day, and the name Irene was later retired because of the damage.

title: Croatia announces the death of President Franjo Tuđman
desc: Croatian state television interrupted its programming at 2 a.m. to announce the death of President Franjo Tuđman, the architect of Croatia’s independence from Yugoslavia and its first president, at 77. He died the night before after six weeks in the hospital, and his death forced a presidential election within 60 days.
